extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, critics, and practitioners studying the mechanisms of humor/ comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical analysis of the mechanisms that make words, sentences, situations, and characters comic; intended to identify recurring devices (repetition, inversion, transposition, automatism, etc.) and how they produce laughter. Useful for literary critics, playwrights, and humor theorists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of events become comic by three methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of events may become comic either by repetition, by inversion, or by reciprocal interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To take series of events and repeat them in another key or environment, invert them while leaving meaning, or mix them so their meanings jostle, is comic because it treats life as if it were mechanical. Applies to sequences of actions and, analogously, to series of words or phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic transformation of sentences (three laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase is likely to become comic if, though reversed, it still makes sense, or if it expresses equally well two independent sets of ideas, or if it is obtained by transposing an idea into some key other than its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are described as the three fundamental laws of THE COMIC TRANSFORMATION OF SENTENCES (inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition). Examples and further subtypes follow in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (sentence reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: INVERSION: putting, for instance, the subject in place of the object and the object in place of the subject to obtain a new (comic) meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised as the least interesting but easy to apply; commonly used by wits and comedians to refute or make fun of an idea (example from Labiche).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference (double-meaning in one sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE: bracketing in the same expression two independent meanings that apparently tally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an inexhaustible source of amusement and includes a range from puns to true play upon words; it relies on one sentence expressing two sets of ideas that interfere with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun (homophonic bribery)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the pun, the same sentence appears to offer two independent meanings, but in reality there are two different sentences made up of different words, claiming to be one because both have the same sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the least reputable way of producing reciprocal interference. Distinguished from 'true play upon words' which uses one sentence whose words have multiple meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: True play upon words (polysemy within one sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true play upon words is one and the same sentence through which two different sets of ideas are expressed, taking advantage of the different meanings a word may have (literal vs figurative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often close to poetic metaphor or illuminating comparison; the play upon words betrays a momentary LAPSE OF ATTENTION in language and that lapse is precisely what makes it amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (moving expression into another key)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRANSPOSITION: transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key always yields a comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposition is to language what repetition is to comedy; it includes many stages from buffoonery to refined irony and underlies devices such as parody, exaggeration, mock-heroic, and the elevation or degradation of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (solemn into familiar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transpose the solemn into the familiar and the result is parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody includes describing lofty subjects in trivial or modern terms (example: 'The sky was beginning to change from black to red, like a lobster being boiled.'). It can also mean expressing old-world matters in modern life terms, producing a humorous halo effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation as a comic form
rubrics_metrics.description: DEGRADATION: making something formerly dignified appear mean or base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some philosophers define the comic generally as degradation; Bergson notes degradation is only one form of transposition and not the sole source of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (speaking of small as large)
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak of small things as though they were large is, in a general way, TO EXAGGERATE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration is always comic when prolonged and systematic; it is a form of transposition and has produced mock-heroic poems and characters whose methodical exaggeration (braggadocio) is laughable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition upwards (describing low things in respectable terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing disreputable ideas or low-class behaviour in the utmost 'RESPECTABILITY' is generally comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often yields strong effect even with brief expression (a single word can reveal a whole system of transposition); common in Dickens, Thackeray, Gogol; English literature often uses this device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between physical size and moral value
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition may operate on either the PHYSICAL DIMENSIONS of an object (size) or on its MORAL VALUE (esteem/respectability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both upward and downward transpositions (exaggeration, degradation) fall under this contrast and produce different comic effects depending on direction and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs Ideal transposition: Irony and Humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrast between the real and the ideal yields two main forms: Irony (we state what ought to be and pretend it is what is) and HUMOUR (we describe what is and pretend that it is what ought to be).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is oratorical and can become high-pressure eloquence; humour is scientific, delights in concrete terms and technical details, and is a transposition from the moral to the scientific (a humorist is a moralist disguised as a scientist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional jargon transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into a professional or business vocabulary produces comic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include using technical or commercial formulas in social contexts (e.g., 'Your kindness of the third ult.'), revealing character traits and sometimes moral faults when social relations are treated as business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language reveals character; comic in words merges with comic in character
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiarities of language often express peculiarities of character and the comic in words merges into comic in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At some point the comic effect in language becomes a disclosure of character rather than mere linguistic play; deeper analysis of such cases is promised in following chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy arises from unsociability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any individual is comic who automatically goes his own way without troubling himself about getting into touch with the rest of his fellow-beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions as social correction ('social ragging') that reproves absentmindedness and lack of adaptability to society. Unsociability (withdrawal into self) is central to the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter is corrective/social (humiliating intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter always implies an unavowed intention to humiliate, and consequently to correct our neighbour, if not in his will, at least in his deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is neither wholly art nor wholly life; its pleasure is not purely aesthetic but carries a social corrective function.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic appeals to intelligence, not to emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic appeals to the intelligence, pure and simple; laughter is incompatible with emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a depiction arouses sympathy, fear, or pity, it cannot be laughed at. The comic poet works to prevent emotional contagion so the audience remains detached and amused rather than moved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing sympathy by isolating feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: One method to make something comic is ISOLATING within the soul of the character the feeling attributed to him, making it a parasitic organism with independent existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a feeling is isolated and rigid instead of permeating the personality, sympathy is blocked and the resulting puppet-like, automatic expression becomes laughable (example: Harpagon forgetting serious matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture over action in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: INSTEAD OF CONCENTRATING OUR ATTENTION ON ACTIONS, COMEDY DIRECTS IT RATHER TO GESTURES (attitudes, movements, language that express a mental state outwardly without aim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gesture is automatic, isolated, and explosive; it rouses sensibility briefly and prevents taking matters seriously. Action is intentional and tied to drama; focusing on gestures produces comic effect (Tartuffe example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism and absentmindedness as comic sources
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically: automatism, absentmindedness, involuntary gestures and unconscious remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic absentmindedness (e.g., Don Quixote) is highly comic. Comic effect often comes from contradictions where a character condemns a conduct and immediately exemplifies it, exposing obliviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters become comic when they crystallise into types
rubrics_metrics.description: Every comic character is a type; every resemblance to a type has something comic in it. Depicting general types (stock characters) is the object of high-class comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy aims at the general and the ready-made element in personality; to be like a known hero or to become a category oneself is comic. This distinguishes comedy from other arts that focus on individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity / ready-made habit causes laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid, the ready-made, the mechanical (in contrast with supple, ever-changing life), absentmindedness versus attention, automatism versus free activity are the defects that laughter singles out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language and persons that are stereotyped or mechanically habitual invite comic treatment; the comic is proportional to rigidity in personality or expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious faults may be laughed at if emotion is not aroused
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious vice or virtue may become ludicrous provided it does not arouse our feelings; it must not touch our emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Harpagon's avarice or Alceste's earnestness; the comic effect depends on preventing emotional engagement so the trait can be seen as rigid/unsociable rather than tragic or admirable.
